sections.h2: Who sends the property tax bill in Seminole County?
sections.html:
Two elected offices split the work in Seminole County. The Seminole County Property Appraiser sets the value and decides exemptions, and the Seminole County Tax Collector mails the bill and takes the payment.

Florida gives every county the same set of constitutional officers, so the layout will look familiar if you have owned elsewhere in the state. The clerk of the circuit court records the deed and collects documentary stamp tax when a sale is recorded. Keep those three roles straight and you will know which counter to call when a question comes up during a sale.

  • Value, exemptions, portability and classifications: the property appraiser.
  • Bills, payments, installment plans, deferral applications and tax certificates: the tax collector.
  • Deed recording and stamp tax: the clerk.

sections.h2: What does Seminole County look like for a home seller?
sections.html:
Seminole County had about 491,884 residents on the Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate, spread over roughly 309 square miles of land. That works out to 1,521.9 people per square mile in the 2020 count.

The 2020 to 2024 Census data show a median owner-occupied value of $386,900 and an owner-occupancy rate of 66.2 percent. Median household income was $85,761. About 18.3 percent of residents are 65 or older, which matters because several Florida tax breaks start at that age. The table below collects the numbers a seller is most likely to want.

sections.h2: Which Seminole County property tax dates should a seller know?
sections.html:
The calendar runs on the same rhythm each year, and the property appraiser's own date page lists it. Ownership and condition on January 1 fix the assessment, and the homestead or agricultural classification filing deadline is March 1.

Personal property returns are due April 1. Notices of proposed taxes (TRIM notices) go out in mid-August, and the window to petition the Value Adjustment Board closes 25 days after that mailing. Value Adjustment Board hearings begin in November, the same month tax bills reach mailboxes.

  • January 1: assessment date for all property.
  • March 1: homestead and agricultural filing deadline.
  • April 1: personal property returns.
  • Mid-August: TRIM notices; 25 days to petition.
  • November: bills mailed, hearings begin.

sections.h2: How does the early payment discount work in Seminole County?
sections.html:
Paying early earns a discount that shrinks each month. The county's appraiser page prints it as 4 percent in November, 3 percent in December, 2 percent in January and 1 percent in February, matching the statewide schedule.

A seller who closes in the fall should find out from the title agent whether the bill has already been paid and at which discount level. If the closing falls in a month with a larger discount, the buyer and seller may want to agree who captures it. Unpaid taxes turn delinquent April 1, and the tax collector then sells tax certificates on unpaid items by June 1 under Florida's statutes. Ask the Seminole County Tax Collector about installment plans and whether the postmark counts, since the state allows an installment application by May 1 of the assessment year.

sections.h2: What happens to Save Our Homes and homestead when a Seminole County house sells?
sections.html:
A sale resets the assessment. Florida treats any sale or transfer of title as a change of ownership, so the property returns to just (market) value on the following January 1 and the seller's capped value does not pass to the buyer.

The seller, though, can keep the cap benefit. Portability lets a homeowner carry the difference between just value and assessed value, up to $500,000, to a new Florida homestead. The state revenue department says the new homestead must be established within three years, and the portability form goes in with the homestead application by March 1. The same Save Our Homes cap limits yearly growth to the lower of 3 percent or the change in the consumer price index, which for 2026 was 2.7 percent on the state's chart.

Homestead also ends if the owner rents the house or moves out. Anyone leaving a Seminole County house for a rental period should speak with the property appraiser first.

sections.h2: What closing costs come from the deed in Seminole County?
sections.html:
The main government charge is documentary stamp tax on the deed, set at 70 cents per $100 of consideration in every county but Miami-Dade, including Seminole. The state revenue department says all parties to the deed are liable regardless of who agrees to pay, so the sale contract should say who pays.

The clerk collects the tax when recording. Recording charges come from the state fee statute: $5.00 for the first page, $4.00 for each additional page, plus modernization and technology charges set in the same section. Consideration includes any mortgage the buyer takes over, so a payoff figure matters. A deed from a personal representative under a probated will is listed by the department as not taxable, which can matter for inherited homes.

sections.h2: What if the Seminole County tax bill is unpaid when you sell?
sections.html:
The unpaid bill does not block a sale, but the buyer's title company will require it paid from proceeds. If a tax certificate was already sold, the owner must clear that as well.

Certificates are sold to the investor who bids the lowest interest rate, in quarter-percent steps. The holder cannot contact the owner for payment until two years after April 1 of the issuance year, and a tax deed application can only follow after that period. Homestead owners get one protection: a homestead with under $250 delinquent must be issued to the county rather than auctioned. Ask the tax collector for a payoff figure before listing so no surprise reaches the closing table.

  • Order a current payoff from the tax collector.
  • Ask the title agent to check for certificates.
  • Confirm who holds any mortgage escrow account.

sections.h2: Can Seminole County owners get help with the tax bill?
sections.html:
Yes. The standard homestead exemption is up to $50,000, with the first $25,000 applying to school taxes too and the second slice applying to non-school taxes on value over $50,000. The additional amount adjusts annually for inflation.

Owners 65 or older may qualify for more where a county or city ordinance allows it and household income is within the limit, so ask the property appraiser which local ordinances apply. Veterans with a service-connected disability of 10 percent or more get a $5,000 assessment reduction, and a total and permanent service-connected disability can bring a total exemption on homestead. Homestead tax deferral is available on application to the tax collector by March 31 for taxes above 5 percent of household income.

faqs.q: Does a Seminole County sale trigger a reassessment?
faqs.a: Yes. Florida treats a sale as a change of ownership, so the property goes to just value the next January 1 and prior caps and exemptions do not carry to the buyer.

faqs.q: When are Seminole County tax bills mailed?
faqs.a: In November, by the county tax collector. Value Adjustment Board hearings also begin that month, and TRIM notices precede both in mid-August.

faqs.q: Where do I file a homestead exemption in Seminole County?
faqs.a: With the Seminole County Property Appraiser, by March 1 of the tax year, on Form DR-501 or the office's own filing. You must have made the home your permanent residence by January 1.

faqs.q: How long do I have to challenge my value in Seminole County?
faqs.a: Twenty-five days after the TRIM notice is mailed in mid-August. File the petition with the Value Adjustment Board through the clerk, using one of the DR-486 forms.

faqs.q: Who pays documentary stamp tax when I sell a Seminole County house?
faqs.a: The law makes every party to the deed liable, so the sale contract should name who pays. The rate is 70 cents per $100 of consideration, collected by the clerk when the deed is recorded.
